RNA, there may have regulatory regions, there could be splices, and so on. For a sequence with thousands of nucleotides, directly superposing on to all the start and stop codons, the correct triplet reading-frames, the intron-exon boundaries, regulatory regions, and so on, is impracticable. It probably makes more sense to leave the sequence in its raw form and add supplementary notes and instructions; but just how much information should we require?

To start, it might be helpful to know what the sequence is and where it came from, in both terms of its location in the genomic sequence and of its source origin. For the example above, we gain useful information from knowing that it is genomic DNA of human origin, and that is derived from the α-globin gene line, which is 1,138 nucleotide bases in length:

> source: genomic DNA, alpha-globin gene line, bases 1–1138
organism: Homo sapiens

This is useful, but it hasn't identified which the primary transcript and the name of the translated protein. We could do this in the following way, so as, at a glance, that there are three exons in the primary transcript, laying bases between 98 and 929:

> primary transcript: 98–929 (exon 1, 98–230; exon 2, 348–551; exon 3, 92–929)
product: alpha globin

By noting features like this, we add increasing value to our raw sequence, such that we can re-use the information quickly and conveniently. The more notes, or annotations, the richer the content. But there's a catch. There are many different ways in which annotations could be arranged in a plan. If we want to use the information again in a particular way, how might we determine which to add; or, if we thought of other potential uses of the information (things that perhaps we don't want to do now, but might want to do in future), this might make us add the notes in a different way, or it might make us consider how to accommodate different kinds of annotation in future.

This is the heart of the matter. As we mentioned in the opening pages of the book, the first biological databases were created to address particular needs at that time, with no idea of the data-generation revolutions ahead. Hence, how the data were stored
